extracted.intended_audience: 16-year-old Americans (youth planning careers), parents and educators
extracted.subtask_description: Short-form career guidance for American teenagers (around age 16) on how to prepare for and succeed in the changing U.S. economy. Advises on education, pursuing passion, manufacturing/technical skills, and location choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get educated
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The changing economy creates an 'iron law of wages': the more you learn, the more you earn. Between 1990 and 2009, median annual earnings fell for workers with a high school education or less and grew for those with a bachelor’s degree or more; workers with a BA or higher earned nearly 80 percent more than those with just a high school diploma in 2009. In the current recovery, education is critical to employment: unemployment rate for those with a BA is 4.3%, compared to 8.2% for some college/associate's, 9.6% for high school, and 14.3% for less than high school. (Use this data to prioritize formal education and credential-building.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow your passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Second, follow your passion. Given the role of work in our lives, it’s best to combine vocation and avocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate personal interests into sectors and roles that will grow in the 21st-century economy. Examples given: if interested in travel, engage in international exchange to connect with rapidly developing countries; if environmentally conscious, pursue sustainable-growth fields (clean tech, organic farming, energy-efficient products, low-carbon cities) to 'do well and do good'; if you like to tinker, participate in technological acceleration—from idea generation to producing and deploying inventions. Example consumer- and city-focused products: smart homes, remote health care, self-driving vehicles, small cars, energy-saving technology. (Choose passions that map to market demand and scalable innovation opportunities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't be afraid to make stuff
rubrics_metrics.description: Third, don’t be afraid to make stuff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturing and innovation are tightly linked: producing goods fuels innovation. Policymakers have de-emphasized manufacturing, but to prosper the U.S. 'must make things again.' As baby boomers leave the manufacturing workforce, skills gaps are emerging: a National Association of Manufacturers study found 32% of industrial companies reported 'moderate to serious' skills shortages, including 63% of life science companies and 45% of energy firms. If you are good with your hands or have technical capacity for advanced manufacturing, find a place to excel producing something that can be proudly stamped 'Made in USA.' (Emphasize hands-on/technical skills and consider advanced manufacturing careers.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Place matters
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The next economy will be differentiated across places; cities can leverage distinctive assets and attributes. Think of work as the product of an ecosystem of innovative firms, talented workers, supportive research institutions, and intermediaries. Seek the right place with the amenities you want and a 'thick' labor market—where relevant firms, talent, and institutions cluster—because opportunity will naturally follow. (Select location strategically to maximize network effects and local industry demand.)
